country.comment: Fieldwork and case study were conducted in Kibera informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya, situated within a broader conceptual discussion of urban governance in Africa.

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative ethnographic case study; descriptive operational figures (e.g., ~50 bio-centres planned/implemented in Kibera, ~600 daily users at Tosha, estimated 100 daily user capacity at Jasho Letu, 2–3 KES user fee) are reported without inferential statistical effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Participatory CBO–NGO partnerships under the Kenya Slum Upgrading Programme (KENSUP) introduced communal sanitation/water bio-centres (charging 2–3 Kenyan shillings per toilet/shower use, with the flagship Tosha bio-centre serving an average of 600 users daily), but sustained water and sanitation access depended on navigating post-construction bureaucratic and governance barriers: a spin-off CBO bio-centre (Jasho Letu, capacity 100 users/day) experienced operational delays because Nairobi City Water Services would not connect its main water pipe for a 10,000-litre tank without written permission from the local chief and clearance across a multi-tier administrative hierarchy; a youth CBO bio-centre (KILYO) lacking post-construction management support and regulation experienced illicit drug-dealing until NGO intervention; and lack of gender-customised design and municipal street lighting prevented women from using bio-centres after dark. Effective service provision required ongoing co-production in which CBOs and NGOs enrolled municipal planners (Nairobi City Council) and state gatekeepers into post-construction permitting, water pipe connections, street lighting coordination, and operational monitoring.

evidence_quotes.quote: Drawing on a case study of the informal sanitation infrastructure known as a bio-centre, which has been introduced by a participatory upgrading programme in Nairobi, Kenya, this article proposes to pay attention to ways that informal settlers experience infrastructure, embed it into their everyday context of place-making and use it in unplanned manners.
Between July 2011 and February 2013, I intermittently visited Kibera slum’s eight major bio-centres, interviewing on average ﬁve members of each CBO.

evidence_quotes.criterion: mechanism_flags and outcome_flags (formal water connection, permits, bureaucratic procedures)
evidence_quotes.quote: After construction, however, the CBO needed to learn to deal with bureaucratic procedures to connect their bio-centre’s water pipe to the city’s ofﬁcial supply grid and to arrange a permit to build different components of the infrastructure such as the water tank.
Once the centre is built, the CBO charges a fee of about 2–3 Kenyan shillings (approximately $0.02–0.03 in 2015) for toilet or shower use.

evidence_quotes.criterion: mechanism_flags and effect_estimate (state accommodation and co-production)
evidence_quotes.quote: Moreover, as bio-centres are not necessarily placed near street lights, women never go to the bio-centres after dark. Concerns for women’s safety have led the local NGOs to demand even more strongly the participation of the City Council as the sole provider of street lights.
